pillars.label: Prevention
pillars.intro: Prevention is about what can catch fire. The flight tests burned fabrics and plastics such as SIBAL, Nomex and PMMA in BASS, BASS-II and the Saffire experiments. Ask me about a material, an investigation, or how oxygen changes burning.

pillars.label: Flammability & Fire Behavior
pillars.intro: This is how a fire behaves once it starts. The flight tests measured how fast flames spread, and how that changed with oxygen and air flow. Ask me, for example, whether fire spreads faster in space.

pillars.label: Detection
pillars.intro: Smoke is usually the first warning. SAME and SAME-R measured the smoke from overheated spacecraft materials on the station. Ask me why smoke is different in space.

pillars.label: Suppression
pillars.intro: This is about putting a fire out. FLEX and CFI burned fuel droplets while carbon dioxide or helium was added to the chamber. Ask me which gases the experiments added, or what happens to cool flames.

prevention:spacesuit.headline: Materials tested
key_points: The nearest PSI data to a spacesuit's 100 percent oxygen are ACME inside-out flames on the space station, where oxygen of up to 85 percent flowed from the burner: 79 tests in CFI-G and 52 in Flame Design at 80 percent or more.
The closest to spacesuit pressure were 2 Flame Design flames with 85 percent oxygen at 43 kilopascals, about 6.2 psia, against the suit's 4.3 psia.
In those tests the chamber held nitrogen and a fuel gas, so no test was run in a pure-oxygen atmosphere; the highest oxygen in a test atmosphere was 40 percent.

BRE tested the 34 percent oxygen, 8.2 psia atmosphere considered to ease spacewalk preparation, and its authors report that higher oxygen and lower pressure tend to make flames more stable and longer-lasting.
